analysis.one_liner: Removes the court-made shield protecting government officials from lawsuits when they violate constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill had 45 Democratic supporters but never received a hearing or a vote in the House Judiciary Committee, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a government official — most often a police officer — violates your constitutional rights, a judge-created doctrine called "qualified immunity" usually shields that official from paying damages unless you can point to a prior case that clearly established the right. This bill would erase that defense in civil suits under the 1871 civil rights statute, so officials could be held personally liable whenever they violate someone's rights, regardless of whether the right was previously spelled out in a court ruling. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by state and local officials — particularly police officers — would gain a real remedy. Under current law, many such lawsuits are thrown out at the start because the victim cannot cite an earlier case with nearly identical facts. This bill would let juries decide the merits instead.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of rights violations by officials

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds language to 42 U.S.C. 1983 stating that it shall not be a defense that the defendant acted in good faith, believed their conduct was lawful, or that the right was not "clearly established" at the time.

The bill's findings argue that the 1871 statute never contained such a defense and that the Supreme Court created it in 1967 and expanded it in 1982, frustrating Congress's original intent to protect civil rights.
The CRS summary states the doctrine has "severely limited the ability of many plaintiffs to recover damages under section 1983 when their rights have been violated by State and local officials."
The bill applies to suits pending on, or filed after, its effective date, not just new cases.

analysis.who_pays: Government officials, especially law enforcement officers, who would lose their personal shield from damages and could be sued whenever they violate rights. Municipalities and their insurers would likely bear higher litigation and settlement costs, and local governments would face pressure to indemnify and train their employees more carefully.

drawbacks.text: A fair objection is that removing qualified immunity entirely could expose officials to personal liability in genuinely hard situations — a split-second decision during a violent encounter may look unlawful in hindsight even when made reasonably — and courts created the doctrine partly to spare officials such hindsight judging.
Higher litigation exposure for officials would likely be passed on to local governments and their taxpayers through indemnification and insurance costs.

An honest drafting note: the bill text references suits "pending on, or filed after, the effective date of the Ending Qualified Immunity Act of 2021," carrying over language from an earlier Congress's version of the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a person beaten or wrongly arrested by an officer, current law often means no remedy at all, and the bill directly addresses that. The costs are real but manageable: governments already pay settlements in these cases while the officer walks free, so shifting liability toward accountability is a trade most supporters consider worth making. The main design weakness is retroactive application and the drafting carryover from the 2021 version, which a competent committee process would have cleaned up — a process this bill never got.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the bill on April 25, 2023, with 41 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary that same day; the full action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
The bill ended the Congress with 44 cosponsors, all Democrats.
No version of the bill was ever voted on in either chamber of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement officers and other government officials keep the qualified immunity shield that makes it hard for people they injure to recover damages, and the local governments and insurers that share those liabilities keep the status quo as well.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police and officials who keep immunity

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ending Qualified Immunity Act and recruited 44 cosponsors.

for.name: 44 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; all were Democrats, none from the majority party.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup in the committee that controlled its fate.

against.name: Law enforcement unions and associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed ending qualified immunity during prior Congresses and lobbied against it; the bill again reached no committee action in this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and government officials
industries.note: The bill would strip the judicially created shield that protects officials from personal damages liability when they violate constitutional rights. Their interest in keeping that shield runs against the people they harm, who currently often have no remedy.
Local governments and insurers would absorb more litigation and settlement costs, though the costs largely reflect harms they would otherwise escape paying for.
